inline.s: The Bodhisattva further admonished the assembly, saying: “Since ancient times the great sages and great worthies, in explaining the subtle
(elucidating the subtle principle)
and establishing the teaching
(carrying on the work of conversion)

, have been entirely refined and entirely simple. Persons of superior faculty, hearing, awaken; those of middling and inferior faculty, hearing, cultivate; all return to the great Way. But the various writings that came after them busied themselves with verbosity and esoteric talk, so that ordinary folk puzzled over them and formed views, until error was passed on as truth and they sank deep into the perverse
Clutching their darkness while life passed
(clutching these perverse and muddled views until death)
, they were not even aware of it.”

The Bodhisattva further guided the assembly, saying: “Since ancient times, the great sages and great worthies, in elucidating the wonderful principle and carrying on the work of teaching, have been wholly refined and wholly simple. Persons of superior faculty (those of the highest capacity), hearing, awaken; those of middling and inferior faculty, hearing, cultivate; all return to the great Way. But the various writings that came after them, however, devoted themselves to verbosity (stringing together chapter after chapter of stuff) and dark sayings (deliberately mystifying), so that ordinary folk would puzzle over them and form views (puzzling over their doctrines and so forming their own opinions), until error was passed on as truth and they sank deep into the perverse and the eccentric (deviation from the right is called perverse; straying from the center is called eccentric). Thus they clutched to these perverse, muddled views for a lifetime, and were not themselves even aware of it.”

[Wording it into a discourse] The Buddhas and the great patriarchs, the venerable masters, truly recounted the states they had realized and their own experience, exactly as the book says of one who has gone to Yanjing: he tells others how to walk the road, and they are able to reach Yanjing; everything is refined and simple. But from ancient times there have also been not a few who sought fame and reputation (people who had never been to Yanjing), who dug a piece here from the sutras and treatises, picked a bit over there, and then arbitrarily strung it together and embellished it, making grand theses, until fish-eyes were passed off as pearls and true and false became hard to tell. Many deceived students, following these in practice, though they toiled diligently, went in exactly the opposite direction; the more they cultivated, the more deluded they became, afflictions sprouted on every side, they clutched their darkness through life, and wasted their years. Therefore, when reading these “great works,” one should first examine whether their content agrees with the sutras and treatises, and whether their author has genuine power and attainment in practice; only then will one not be led astray. Master Honen’s fishing in troubled waters is a bitter warning of exactly this sort (see
Master Honen’s Forging of the Great Vow Gate
[Such as Daben: because he read the Can Tong
(the Can Tong Qi)
and the Wu Zhen
(the Wu Zhen Pian)
and other books, but did not know the essential teaching, he falsely trusted
(believed recklessly)
the erroneous transmission, thought he had attained, clutched it fondly
(deluded attachment and clinging)

would not let it go. To white hair he had no accomplishment, and various afflictions arose. The Bodhisattva said, these are truly to be pitied. Therefore, since you now recognize your former error, you should reverence right faith.”]

For example, Daben, because he read the Can Tong Qi, the Wu Zhen Pian, and other such books, did not know the true essential teaching, but falsely believed the erroneous transmission, thinking he had some attainment, and clung to it fondly, unable to let it go. As a result, to white hair he had no accomplishment, and afflictions sprouted on every side. The Bodhisattva said: these misled beings are truly pitiable! Therefore, since you have now recognized your former error, you ought to reverence right faith.”
[At one time, the Bodhisattva was about to come to the Dharma assembly. Eight disciples — Wuxiu, Changshe, Changyuan, Dingmao, Daben, Zha Dinghong, Chen Dingzhuan, and Zha Dingmin — reverently gazing
yóng
, the look of admiring reverence)
stood
zhù
, standing for a long time)
, and together chanted the Buddha’s name. Suddenly a wondrous fragrance came from the sky; all were delighted and had never known such a thing.]

At one time, the Bodhisattva was about to come to the Dharma assembly, and eight disciples — Wuxiu, Changshe, Changyuan, Dingmao, Daben, Zha Dinghong, Chen Dingzhuan, and Zha Dingmin — stood reverently and chanted the Buddha’s name together. Suddenly a wondrous fragrance came from the sky, and the whole assembly was greatly delighted, having never experienced such a thing.

[The Bodhisattva said: “Excellent! Excellent! Do you know that this assembly today has a condition from past lives? In the sixth year of the Tianjian era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, I left home at the Jingyin Temple in the eastern capital of the Northern Wei, as a great bhikshu. Because of the turmoil of war I journeyed south, and took up my staff at the foot of Jiming Mountain
(the mountain’s foot)

. At that time, you eight relied on me in study and practice, but before long the war scattered us each on our way. Two years after that I passed away at Tianzhu in Wulin. Later, in the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang, I was the eldest son of Prince Xian of Qinghe, and likewise abandoned rank to leave home. Now you eight, gathered together to recite the Buddha’s name, also came about through my stirring the resolve, exactly as in former times. But since you eight left me, more than eight hundred years have passed, and you are still drifting without return — truly pitiable, truly painful! Now for you I shall again set forth clearly the practice you have cultivated, that you may quickly accomplish it and soon attain liberation. Each of you should listen attentively.”]
The Bodhisattva said: “Excellent! Excellent! Do you know that this assembly today has a condition from past lives. Formerly, in the sixth year of the Tianjian era of Emperor Wu of the Liang (

), I left home at the Jingyin Temple, the eastern capital of the Northern Wei, as a great bhikshu. Because of the turmoil of war I journeyed south and rested my staff at the foot of Jiming Mountain. At that time, you eight relied on me in study and practice, but not long after the war scattered us each apart. Two years later I passed away at Tianzhu in Wulin. Later, in the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang (

), I was the eldest son of Prince Xian of Qinghe, and likewise abandoned my rank to leave home. Now you eight, gathered together to recite the Buddha’s name, also came about through my stirring the resolve, exactly as of old. But since you eight left me, more than eight hundred years have passed, and you are still transmigrating ceaselessly in the six realms — truly pitiable, truly painful! Now for you I shall set forth clearly the path of practice, that you may quickly attain the Way and soon be liberated. Each of you should now concentrate your mind and listen attentively.”
[Resting the staff]
A monk taking up residence in a place. The staff is the khakkhara.
[Passing away]
A term for the death of a Buddha, a Bodhisattva, or an eminent monk. “Passing away” means entering still nirvana; as a manifestation of nirvana, it is not a true extinction.

blocks.text: Diligent Practice of the Pure Karma

inline.s: [Addressing Wuxiu, he said: “Though formerly you pursued the esoteric path, yet you were able to revere the Buddhas; know that this is a condition from former lives. Now you should quickly rouse a deep resolve and diligently practice the pure karma, leading the others in the right way
(that is, to lead and set the example)

. Do not waste these thirteen years that yet remain to you. I give you a verse: Eight hundred years ago was a goodly bond; today we meet, and I point to the blue sky. You know already the mid-autumn moon of this very ground; do not seek a ferryboat upon the long river.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Wuxiu, saying: “Though formerly you pursued the esoteric path, yet you could revere the Buddhas; know that this is a condition from former lives. Now you should quickly arouse a deep resolve and diligently practice the pure karma, leading the assembly to cultivate on the right path. Do not squander the thirteen years of life still left to you! I give you a verse:
Eight hundred years ago, a goodly bond (eight hundred years ago we were master and disciple),
Today we meet, and I point to the blue sky (causing you to see the moon — the true great Way),
You know already the mid-autumn moon of this very ground (a metaphor: since you already know the most appropriate great Way — the Pure Land teaching),
Do not seek a ferryboat upon the long river (then do not go seeking a boat to search out another land’s moon; a metaphor for not seeking any other path of practice).”

[Addressing Changshe, he said: “You always hold the Great Compassion Dharani — how do you hold it?” He replied: “The mantra I hold is distinct and clear; the mind that holds it is entirely ungraspable.” The Bodhisattva said: “To hold it thus is called true holding. I give you a verse: You hold the Great Compassion Mantra; you should know the Great Compassion mind — apart from name and apart from mark, and thereby cross over the multitude of beings.”]

To Changshe he instructed: “You always hold the Great Compassion Dharani — how do you hold it?” Changshe replied: “The mantra I hold is distinct and clear; the mind that holds it is entirely ungraspable.” The Bodhisattva said: “To be able to hold it thus is called true holding. I give you a verse in charge to you: You hold the Great Compassion Mantra; you should know the Great Compassion mind — apart from name and apart from mark, and thereby (uniting compassion and emptiness) cross over the multitude of beings.”
[Addressing Changyuan, he said: “Since you have already left home, you must
(be sure to)

be humble and gentle, reverence and serve your teachers and elders, empty yourself and ask for instruction, and increase your resolve — do not merely sit in the clouds and fog passing your days.” Yuan did not understand
(Changyuan did not comprehend)
. Again he said: “Muddled
mèng méng
, dim and confused)

as you are, can you know your own mind?” Yuan was speechless. So he had him recite the Cundi mantra once, and Yuan recited it accordingly. The Bodhisattva said: “Is this not your mind? What would you call it? A verse: See the firstless, mindless state; this is your original mind. Recite Cundi once, and the whole body is clear.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Changyuan, saying: “Since you have already left home, be sure to be humble and gentle, reverence and serve your teachers and elders, empty yourself and seek instruction, and increase your resolve — do not merely sit in the clouds and fog, muddled, passing your days.” Changyuan did not understand. The Bodhisattva again instructed: “Dim and confused as you are, can you know your own mind?” Changyuan could not answer. (If Changyuan did not even know his own mind, where was he to begin cultivation? So below the Bodhisattva tells him what the mind is.) Thereupon he had Changyuan recite the Cundi mantra once, and Changyuan recited it accordingly. The Bodhisattva said: “Is this not your mind? What would you call it? I give you a verse: See the firstless, mindless state; this is your original mind; recite Cundi once, and the whole body is clear.”
[The Cundi mantra] Namo sadu nan
nā mó sà duō nán
, samyaksambudha
sān miǎo sān pú tuó
koti nan
jù zhī nán,
tadyatha
dá zhí tuō,
om cale cule
ǎn/ōng, zhé lì zhŭ lì,
cundi svaha
zhūn tí suō pó hē.

[This is not your mind — what would you call it?] The mind is the functioning of the self-nature. Changyuan recited the Cundi mantra, and the Bodhisattva immediately said: “Is this not your mind? What would you call it?” Therefore, reciting the mantra is just one’s own mind setting itself to work. Likewise, when one gives rise to confused thoughts, greed, anger, and delusion, it is also one’s own mind setting itself to work. Only, in the former case it is aware, in the latter it is deluded. [See the firstless, mindless state; this is your original mind; recite Cundi once, and the whole body is clear] The meaning of this verse is: seeing the mind that at first is without thought — this is your original mind (no-thought is the original mind; having thought is the consciousness mind); recite the Cundi mantra once, and one should make the mantra within the mind distinct and clear (the whole body clear); if so, one is not sitting in the clouds and fog, muddled, passing one’s days.
[Addressing Dingmao, he said: “You hold the Cundi mantra; in daily life you must apply the mind minutely. Observe all states, whether clamorous or still
(whether noisy or silent)

, whether things or not-things, whether pleasing or repugnant — all are nothing but this mantra manifesting itself, which is my wonderful mind flowing forth at every moment. Holding it thus, you will certainly attain the fruit; and I will also aid you to accomplishment with spiritual power. You should recite my verse: Two lines
(pointing to the Cundi mantra)
of secret, this is your original mind; do not say the Dharma is slight — this Dharma is very deep.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Dingmao, saying: “You hold the Cundi mantra; in daily life you must apply the mind minutely. Observe all states, whether clamorous or still, whether things or not-things, whether pleasing or repugnant — all are nothing but this mantra manifesting itself without being pulled along by the state; this is one’s own wonderful mind flowing forth at every moment. Holding it thus, you will certainly attain the fruit of realization, and I will also aid you to accomplishment with spiritual power. You should recite my verse: Two lines (pointing to the Cundi mantra) of secret, this is your original mind; do not say the Dharma is slight (do not think the Cundi mantra is only two lines of characters) — this Dharma is very deep.”

[Two lines of secret, this is your original mind] The secret of the Cundi mantra lies in holding it until the original mind manifests before you. [This Dharma is very deep] In holding the mantra there are

three barriers: the ten thousand thoughts returning to one, the samadhi manifesting, and the correct samadhi apart from holding. Master Huiming taught: “What is the first barrier? When a practitioner holds the mantra and reaches the point where ten thousand thoughts return to one, no second thought arising, this is called passing the first barrier. But this is pressing down the grass with a stone — not yet the ultimate. What is the second barrier? When the mantra is held to the point of holding without holding, and not holding while holding, and who it is that holds, one does not even know, even as it seems two persons are holding at once — this is called the samadhi manifesting, also called passing the second barrier. What is the third barrier? When the mantra is held to the point where true, false, and Dharma, all three, are unknown, and one enters deep samadhi, attaining the correct samadhi apart from holding — having nothing at all, one realizes the reality-mark, all things complete — this is called passing the third barrier.” (See
Master Huiming’s Recorded Instructions
.) These are also the three barriers of Buddha-recitation, passing from the one mind of practice into the one mind of principle.

[Observe all states, whether clamorous or still, whether things or not-things, whether pleasing or repugnant — all are nothing but this mantra manifesting itself, which is my wonderful mind flowing forth at every moment] The ten thousand dharmas are empty and still; the mantra-body is empty and still; the wonderful mind is empty and still — three and yet one. This is the state of holding the mantra into the reality-mark, the one mind of principle. Because beginning students find it hard to grasp, the text has not been explained in this way; if a practitioner’s work approaches this, there is no need of explanation, and one can of oneself comprehend the Bodhisattva’s instruction. The phrase “two lines of secret, this is your original mind” in the verse below is likewise this situation. Hence Mr. Peng Shaosheng, in his postface, praises it: “Elucidating the wondrous purport of the one mind, exhausting the mystery of the upward-turning gate.”

[He asked Daben: “What will you do?” He replied: “I wish to understand the mind.” The Bodhisattva said: “Is that not empty talk of the mouth? You should diligently recite the Buddha’s name; its merit is tenfold. I also give you a verse: apart from the mind there is no Buddha; the Buddha is your very mind; believe deeply and be not confused; in a single thought, no birth.”]

The Bodhisattva asked Daben: “What do you intend to do?” Daben replied: “I wish to understand the mind and see the nature.” The Bodhisattva said: “Is this not a stock phrase of the mouth? You should diligently recite the Buddha’s name; its merit is tenfold that of your mouth-talk. I give you a verse too: apart from the mind there is no Buddha; the Buddha is your very mind; believe deeply and be not confused; in a single thought, no birth.”
[Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; the Buddha is your very mind] Concerning the principle of “just this mind, just this Buddha,” one may refer to
The Annotated Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

[Addressing Zha Dinghong, he said: “You hold the Diamond Prajna; you should know there are seven not-holdings, namely: when the mind is scattered and dull, do not hold; when there has been offense, do not hold; after entering an impure place, do not hold; after drinking wine, do not hold; when disturbed by people and not pure, do not hold; when a matter is about to be done and not yet done, do not hold; when the mind is occupied with other recollection, do not hold. If you are firmly resolved to hold and recite, you should be apart from these seven; and when you have recited to full familiarity, hold it within the contemplative mind. If you can do this, then the merit is inconceivable, and the retribution is inconceivable. The Buddha has a sincere word; you must guard and sustain it. Again I give you a verse: the Prajna sutra — its merit is without end; it pulls up the root of deluded thought, and delivers from the sickness of birth and death.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Zha Dinghong, saying: “You hold the Diamond Sutra; you should know there are seven not-holdings, namely: when the mind is scattered and dull, do not hold; when there has been offense, do not hold; after entering an impure place, do not hold; after drinking wine, do not hold; when disturbed by people and not pure, do not hold; when a matter is about to be done and not yet done, do not hold; when the mind is occupied with other recollection, do not hold. If you are firmly resolved to hold and recite, you should be apart from these seven items; and when you have recited to full familiarity, hold it within the contemplative mind. If you can truly do this, then the merit is inconceivable, and the retribution is inconceivable. The Buddha has a sincere word; you must surely guard and sustain it. Again I give you a verse: the Prajna scripture (pointing to the Diamond Sutra) — its merit is without end; it pulls up the root of deluded thought, and delivers from the sickness of birth and death.”
[The Buddha has a sincere word]

The merit and virtue of holding, reciting, and reading the Diamond Sutra are extremely vast, and its retribution is inconceivable; the Buddha speaks of it repeatedly in the Diamond Sutra. For example: “In the future age, if good men and good women are able, with regard to this sutra, to hold, recite, and read it, the Tathagata, with Buddha-wisdom, knows all such persons and sees all such persons, and they will all accomplish immeasurable, boundless merit.” “If a person is able to hold, recite, and read it, and widely proclaim it to others, the Tathagata knows all such persons and sees all such persons, and they will all accomplish merit that is immeasurable, uncountable, without bounds, and inconceivable. Such persons as these will bear the burden of the Tathagata’s anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.” “In the future age, at the end of five hundred years, if there are beings who hear this sutra, believe, understand, accept, and hold it, then such persons are the foremost and most rare.”
[Guard and sustain]

Protection and free flowing, the two stages of removing habitual tendencies after seeing the nature. “Protection” means to take every care of the holy embryo so that it is not harmed; “free flowing” means that after the holy embryo has matured into a full-grown man, it follows the circumstances and conditions and operates of itself, being further tempered amid favorable and adverse conditions.

[Addressing Chen Dingzhuan, he said: “The petty person does evil and only fears that others know; the noble person does good and likewise only fears that others know. You should use the mind of the noble person who is careful in the Way, and do Buddha’s work. Further, there is a verse: do not ask that others know; do not hope for heaven’s response; constantly unify your mind — it must be firm and upright.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Chen Dingzhuan, saying: “The petty person does evil and only fears that others know; the noble person does good and likewise only fears that others know. You should use the mind of the noble person who is careful in the Way, and do Buddha’s work. Further, there is a verse for you: do not ask that others know; do not hope for heaven’s response; constantly unify your mind — it must be firm and upright.”
[Careful in the Way] In all matters one must carefully and cautiously act according to the Way, and not turn away from it.

[Addressing Zha Dingmin, he said: “You are not yet twenty, and already you know to seek the Way; this shows a former condition. Now I name you ‘Min’; the character ‘Min’ has four meanings: keen, diligent, subtle, and quick. Keenness to dispel your darkness, diligence to spur your sloth, subtlety to open your wisdom, quickness
(swiftness)
to stir your neglect
(idleness)

. You should bethink yourself of the meaning when you hear the name, and do not think the Bodhisattva gave you a word for nothing. Further, I give you a verse: you are young indeed; you should learn filial piety and fraternal respect, and with these hold your body upright — do not be slack in your resolve.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Zha Dingmin, saying: “You have not yet reached twenty, and already you know to seek the Way; one can see that this is a former condition. Now I name you ‘Min’; the character ‘Min’ has four meanings: keen, diligent, subtle, and quick. Keenness dispels your darkness; diligence spurs your sloth; subtlety opens your wisdom; quickness guards against your idleness. You should bethink yourself of the meaning when you hear the name, and do not think the Bodhisattva gave you a single word for nothing. Further, I give you a verse: you are young indeed; you should learn filial piety and fraternal respect, and with these hold your body upright — do not slacken your resolve.”

[Not yet twenty] The age before twenty. “Weak crown”: in ancient times a male assumed the cap at twenty; because he had not yet reached strength of years, it was called the weak crown. [Filial and fraternal] Written also “xiaoti” (
tì
): being filial to parents and respectful to elder brothers.

[That day, Chen Daxin arrived late. The Bodhisattva asked him: “How do you cultivate?” He replied: “Only the Pure Land.” The Bodhisattva said: “Apart from this there is no other excellent gate. I enjoin you a verse: The Way has no other saying — only the mind; when the lotus embryo first forms, be single and undivided.”]

That day, Chen Daxin arrived only later. The Bodhisattva asked him: “How do you cultivate?” Chen Daxin answered: “I cultivate only the Pure Land.” The Bodhisattva said: “Apart from this there is no better gate. I enjoin you a verse: The Way has no other saying — only the mind; when the lotus embryo first forms, be single and undivided.”

blocks.text: The Bodhisattva’s Attainment of the Way

inline.s: [The Bodhisattva said: “The gate of the Pure Land that I have shown is truly the mind-ancestry of all Buddhas, the direct path of the human and heavenly realms
(the short road by which the human and heavenly realms escape birth and death)

. Now, though you seek rebirth, if your vow is not resolute, it is like entering the sea and not obtaining the pearl — wasted toil with no benefit. Formerly, in the reign of Emperor Ming of the Jin, I received the body of a poor child. Because of poverty I made a great vow, saying: ‘Because of
(owing to)
former karma
(the karmic offenses of former lives)

, I receive this bitter retribution. If today I do not see Amitabha Buddha and am not born in the Land of Bliss, and do not accomplish all merit, even though I lose this body, I will never retreat nor rest.’ Having made this vow, for seven days and seven nights I single-mindedly recollected, and then my mind opened, and I saw the noble marks and light of Amitabha Buddha, pervading the ten directions. Before the Buddha I personally received the prophecy, and later, at seventy-five, I sat and passed away, and was born in the Land of Bliss.]

The Bodhisattva instructed: “The Pure Land gate I have shown is truly the mind-ancestry of all Buddhas, the direct path by which the human and heavenly realms escape birth and death. Now, though you recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Western Land of Bliss, if your vow is not genuine, it is like entering the sea and not obtaining the pearl — toilsome and of no benefit. In former times, in the reign of Emperor Ming of the Jin (

), I was born as a poor man. Because of poverty, I then made a great vow: ‘Owing to the karmic offenses of my former lives, I receive this bitter retribution. If today I do not see Amitabha Buddha and am not born in the Land of Bliss, and do not accomplish all merit, even though I lose my life, I will never retreat, never rest.’ Having made the vow, for seven days and seven nights I single-mindedly recollected, and then my mind opened, and I saw the noble marks and light of Amitabha Buddha, pervading the ten directions. Before the Buddha I personally received the prophecy, and later, at seventy-five, I sat and passed away, straight to rebirth in the Western Land of Bliss. (From this one knows the Bodhisattva attained the Way in the reign of Emperor Ming of the Jin; his appearances thereafter are all manifestations.)

[Afterward, because his vow to save beings was heavy, he came again to this land, manifesting transformation in accord with each place. Sometimes a bhikshu, sometimes a layman, sometimes a king, sometimes a minister, sometimes a woman, sometimes a butcher or beggar; sometimes hidden, sometimes manifest; sometimes compliant, sometimes adverse — always he taught the Dharma in accordance with beings, guiding all the various kinds. And because those who cultivate the immortal way mostly have not awakened to the true eternal, but are sunk in the bliss of long life and do not think of further progress, I manifested an immortal body to save them from their delusion and fall — as in the affair of the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang. Now again I have set right and wrong before you and proclaimed the Pure Land. You should be of one will and one mind, and firmly cultivate this gate; you will not be misled. If your resolve is once made firm, you need not wait for rebirth in another life to see the Buddha; even now you can see the Buddha, just as I did in former years. I have a verse of four lines: speak one sentence less; recite one thought more of the Buddha’s name; beat the thought to death, and you will be allowed your Dharmakaya to live.”]

Afterward, because his vow to save beings was heavy, he came again to this land, manifesting transformation in accord with each place. Sometimes a bhikshu, sometimes a layman, sometimes a king, sometimes a minister, sometimes a woman, sometimes a butcher or beggar; sometimes hidden, sometimes manifest; sometimes compliant, sometimes adverse — always he taught the Dharma in accordance with beings, guiding and transforming beings of every faculty. And because those who cultivate the immortal way mostly have not awakened to the true eternal, but are sunk in the bliss of long life and do not think of further progress, so I manifested an immortal body to save them from the path of delusion — as in the affair of the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang (as said earlier, the Bodhisattva “in the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang was the eldest son of Prince Xian of Qinghe, and likewise abandoned rank to leave home”). Now again I have set right and wrong clearly before you and proclaimed the Pure Land gate. You should be of one will and one mind, and firmly cultivate this gate; you will not be misled. If your resolve is once made firm, you need not wait for life’s end and rebirth in the Land of Bliss to see Amitabha Buddha; even now you can see Amitabha Buddha, just as I did in former years. I have a verse of four lines: speak one sentence less; recite one thought more of the Buddha’s name; beat the thought to death, and you will be allowed your Dharmakaya to live.”
[Someone asked
(a person asked)

: “How can a practitioner be free of dusty desire and be without hindrance?” The Bodhisattva said: “I shall proceed from the small to the great, and from the outer to the inner; you should well understand the meaning. Suppose someone here, without reason, takes a coin from you — does anger arise?” He answered: “Though a coin is slight, being taken without reason, one is angry.” “Again, if someone gives you a coin without reason, does joy arise?” He said: “Though a coin is slight, being given without reason, one is glad.” One answered: “Since a coin is very slight, what joy is there in being given it? And nothing to be angered at in being taken.”]

A person asked: “How can a practitioner be far from dusty desire and without hindrance?” The Bodhisattva said: “I shall proceed from the small to the great, and from the outer to the inner; you must well understand its meaning. Suppose here someone takes a coin from you without reason — are you angered?” He answered: “Though a coin is small, being taken without reason, of course one is resentful.” The Bodhisattva asked: “Then, if someone gives you a coin without reason, are you pleased?” He answered: “Though a coin is small, being given without reason, of course one is delighted.” One person answered: “A coin is very small; what delight in being given it? And nothing to resent in being taken.”

[The Bodhisattva said: “If you could do this, your mind would long since have been pure; how could you, up to this day, still be sunk in defilement? You should know that practitioners wash their minds not carefully; seeing existence and non-existence, they cling everywhere, and thought after thought is greed, so that karmic consciousness stirs and scatters without a moment’s stop. Even when one recites the name Amitabha Buddha, the mind still wanders abroad, unable for an instant to return to one. This is entirely because, over immeasurable kalpas, you have never for one hour or one day roused the mind to be far from dusty desire; and so this dusty desire, from beginningless kalpas, has never for one hour or one day been willing to leave your minds. Body entwined and mind bound, you sink deep into the net of the dust — how could you be like the lotus emerging from the mud unstained?]

The Bodhisattva said: “If you were already able to do this, your mind would have been pure long ago; why to this day are you still sunk in the muddy defilement? You should know that practitioners wash the mind not finely: seeing existence and non-existence, they are stained everywhere, thought after thought is greed and anger, so that karmic consciousness stirs and scatters without a moment’s pause. Even while reciting the name Amitabha Buddha, the mind still wanders abroad, unable for an instant to return to one. This is all because, over immeasurable kalpas, you have never for one hour or one day roused a mind to be far from dusty desire; and therefore this dusty desire, from beginningless kalpas, has never for one hour or one day been willing to leave your minds. Body entwined and mind bound, you sink deep into the net of the dust — how could you be like the lotus that emerges from the mud unstained?”

[Therefore know that, to cut off greed and clinging, one should first take up the giving and taking of a single coin and practice the contemplation of renunciation, the contemplation that it is not mine. In being taken, no anger rises; in being given, no joy rises. Thus, even to hundreds and thousands of coins, even to billions and trillions of coins, even to cities, kingdoms, wives, and children, even to one’s own flesh, blood, and marrow, even to the mind, will, and consciousness of past, present, and future, even to birth and death, karmic retribution, bodhi, and nirvana — all are no different from the giving and taking of this single coin. Naturally habitual leaks will die away, obstructing conditions be forever extinguished, and one will gradually tread the pure path and accomplish the factors of the Way. You should cultivate according to this; deceive no more and obstruct
(self-deception)
one another and your own
zhì ài
, hindrance and obstruction)

Therefore one knows that, to cut off greed, anger, and clinging, one should first take the giving and taking of a single coin and practice the contemplation of renunciation, the contemplation that it is not mine. In being taken, no anger rises; in being given, no joy rises. Thus, even to hundreds and thousands of coins, even to billions and trillions, even to cities, kingdoms, wives, and children, even to one’s own flesh, blood, and marrow, even to the mind, will, and consciousness of past, present, and future, even to birth and death, karmic retribution, bodhi, and nirvana — all are no different from the giving and taking of this single coin. Naturally habitual tendencies and afflictions die away, obstructing conditions are forever extinguished, and one gradually becomes pure, accomplishing the factors of the Way. You should cultivate according to this, and no longer deceive and obstruct yourselves.”

[Mind, will, and consciousness] Mind has the meaning of gathering and accumulating, and is the eighth consciousness (alaya-vijnana); will has the meaning of deliberation, and is the seventh consciousness (manas-vijnana); consciousness has the meaning of discernment, and is the sixth consciousness. [Leak] A name for affliction, with the two meanings of leaking out and falling away. Greed, anger, and similar afflictions, day and night, flow out ceaselessly from the gates of the six faculties, hence they are called leaks. Moreover, affliction can make a person fall into the three evil realms, hence it is also called a leak.

blocks.text: Setting Offerings and Wishing Long Life

inline.s: [On the second day of early winter
(the first month of winter, the tenth lunar month)
, being the anniversary of the Bodhisattva’s birth, the assembly set out offerings and wished him long life. The Bodhisattva said: “With what do you honor me
(with what do you offer me birthday felicitations)

?” All said: “With the mind as offering.” The Bodhisattva said: “What thing is the mind, that it can be offered?” They replied: “Only the utmost sincerity, which in itself is nothing.” The Bodhisattva said: “Since you say it is nothing, who knows the sincerity? The one who can know the sincerity must have a place, from which it can be shown and pointed out — how can it be ‘nothing’?” They replied: “In truth, there is nothing attained.” The Bodhisattva said: “You say there is no attainment — is this a temporary absence, or a definite absence?” The assembly deliberated and could not answer.]

On the second day of the tenth month, the anniversary of the Bodhisattva’s birth, the assembly set out offerings and wished him long life. The Bodhisattva said: “With what do you offer me birthday felicitations?” All answered: “With the mind as offering.” The Bodhisattva said: “What thing is the mind, such that it can be brought as an offering?” The assembly replied: “Only the utmost sincerity, which in itself is nothing.” The Bodhisattva said: “Since you say it is nothing, who knows it to be sincere? The one who can know the sincerity must have a place, from which it can be discussed and shown — why do you say ‘nothing’?” The assembly replied: “In truth there is nothing attained.” The Bodhisattva said: “You say there is no attainment — is this a temporary absence, or a definite absence?” The assembly deliberated and gave no answer.
[With the mind as offering] To take the mind as offering; the word order is inverted for emphasis.

[The Bodhisattva said: “If it is nothing, then it is definitively nothing; if it is something, then it is definitively something. Once a hair’s doubt intervenes, a hair’s breadth becomes a thousand miles. You should know that when you speak of sincerity or falsity, of existence or non-existence, all these are minds of arising and ceasing, calculation, inference, and speculation. Offering these to me brings no benefit at all. Hear my wonderful verse: The ultimate truth has no dual mind; the ultimate truth has a measureless mind; the mind is not all minds; all natures are not mind. Apart from deluded thought, the mind is not real; relying on the true mind, a name is forced. Neither the true nor the false stand, homage to Shakyamuni the Honored One. Understand that mind has no place; expediently, bring blessings to the multitude of beings.”]
